full_judgment: 49. On discussion of the evidence for both prosecution and defence versions of the case, we are left only with the evidence of PW 1 which is intended to connect these appellants with the murder. The fundamental principle of a criminal trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and that he is not required to adduced evidence to prove his innocence but the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone and till that time the presumption of innocence continues, whether the case is before the trial Court or at higher forums. Again, law does not require a particular number of witnesses to prove a case and conviction may be founded on the testimony of a solitary witness. But rule of prudence, if not rule of law, requires corroboration of such evidence. In this case, there is no question of corroboration unless the evidence of the solitary witness PW 1 is itself found to be trust-worthy. The whole defence case is based on the allegation of false implication of the appellants, particularly of appellant Muslem, the Chairman and appellant Kamini, a member of the Minority-community, who had dared file a Civil Suit against Daroga, PW 6. Upon a simple reading of the judgments of the trial court and the appellate court we find that no attempt has been made to appreciate the defence case vis-a-vis the prosecution case, but the statements of prosecution witnesses given in examination-in-chief have been virtually reproduced in the judgments and accepted without making searching examination of the evidence. In a criminal trial determination of a disputed fact is the main task before the court and such determination is dependent upon consideration of answers given by prosecution witnesses in their cross-examination. Cross-examination is therefore, indispensably necessary bring out desirable facts of a case modifying the examination-in-chief of establishing the cross-examiner's own case. The object of cross-examination in two fold, to bring out the case of the party cross-examining and to impeach the credit of the witness. In examination-in-chief the witness discloses only those facts which are favourable to the party examining him and does not disclose the necessary facts which to in favour of the other side. Cross-examination in a criminal case aims at extraction of the facts which go in favour of the other side. Cross-examination in a criminal case aims at extraction of the facts which support the defence version which is very often sought to be suppressed by the prosecution. The opponents can of course establish facts favourable to them by calling their own witnesses; but "there is something dramatic in proving one's own case from the mouth of the witnesses of the opponent." In this case, excepting the evidence of the defence witnesses in support of the alibi of appellant Nannu, the defence version of the case has came out of the mouth of the prosecution witnesses during their cross-examination, but that version got virtually no consideration from either of the courts below. Test of veracity or credit of a witness is an all-important means of ascertaining the truth of a disputed fact. These courts did not consider the probabilities and circumstances of the case before relying upon the evidence of the single witness, PW 1. These courts did not consider the fact that excepting PWs 4 and 5 neighbouring people including Ahmed, son of the deceased and Ahmed's wife (who came to the spot on the following morning) did not depose in this case. These courts also did not consider the probability of the informant's recognition of so many persons, with detailed description. Both number and nature of the injuries on the dead body hardly support the prosecution case as to participation of so many assailants; rather evidence of PW 2, doctor, and PW 7, who held inquest on the dead body shows only four injuries, two of them in the chest and head are actually the cause of the death; the injuries on the hand and ear are simple. All these injuries could have been easily caused by one or two assailants with daggers as found by PW 7. Introduction of 'long daos' "with narrow ends" brings in some oddity to the matter. Moreover, Idris was a mere bargadar of Khursheda who claimed to have purchased the land already in possession of the appellants except Kamini. By killing the bargadar what benefit these appellants would derive? On the contrary, by securing their conviction in a case of murder, the purchaser, Khursheda would get the real benefit removing all obstructions to her possession. To this may be added the long-standing grudge and humiliation of defeat in election of Abdul Hye whose unseen hand is clearly visible starting from the mysterious arrival of the Daroga on the scene of murder for which the really aggrieved persons, wife or son of the deceased, did not go to the thana. They did not go to the thana, it appears, simply because they did not know who were the assailants. In these circumstances, the defence case of false implication appears to be quite probable.
